title_en: Fragments on the Epistle to Titus
author: Severianus of Gabala
occasion: The surviving fragments come from catena quotations on Titus, addressing interpretive problems in the letter: why Paul cites a pagan poet, how to reconcile purity language with the Creator, and how to apply instructions to women and teachers.
argument: Severianus explains that Paul quotes the Cretan poet's line about Cretans not to endorse the poet's theology but to affirm only the truth about Cretan character, explicitly distancing himself from the poet's false claim about Zeus's tomb. He argues that all things are pure by creation, so impurity lies in human defilement, not in the Creator. He interprets Paul's instruction to older women as showing that women are called to a clerical inheritance, since Paul would not have called them 'reverent' otherwise. He also distinguishes integrity of mind from dignity of work, urging avoidance of corrupt thoughts as well as corrupt deeds.

outline.move: Severianus explains why Paul affirms the Cretan poet's saying as true while distancing himself from the poet's false claim about Zeus's tomb.
He explains why Paul commands sharp rebuke for the Cretans and argues that all things are pure by creation, so impurity cannot be blamed on the Creator.
He quotes the lemma about those who profess to know God but deny him by works, and argues that calling women 'reverent' shows they are called to a clerical inheritance.
He distinguishes integrity of mind from dignity of work, urging avoidance of corrupt thoughts as well as corrupt deeds.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle and author of the Epistle to Titus, whose statements Severianus interprets.

cast.name: the poet (unnamed)
cast.who: The Cretan poet quoted by Paul, identified only as 'the poet' in the fragment; modern scholarship often identifies him as Epimenides, but the source does not name him.

cast.name: Zeus
cast.who: The pagan god whose tomb the poet claimed to show, thereby denying his immortality; Severianus notes the poet 'lied defending Zeus'.

cast.name: Cretans
cast.who: The people of Crete, described by the quoted saying as liars, evil beasts, and idle gluttons.

cast.name: Titus
cast.who: The recipient of the epistle, instructed to rebuke the Cretans sharply.

voices.speaker: the poet (unnamed)
voices.how_marked: Quoted directly in the lemma from Titus 1:12 as 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle gluttons'

voices.speaker: Paul (quoted Scripture)
voices.how_marked: Quoted directly from the Epistle to Titus as lemmata

key_terms.sense: The testimony or witness of the Cretan poet about Cretans, which Paul affirms as true in a limited sense
Liars, the first charge in the quoted saying against Cretans
Idle gluttons, the third charge in the quoted saying, describing Cretan character
Sharply or severely, the manner in which Titus is to rebuke the Cretans
Pure, referring to all things as created by God and to the pure in heart
Reverent or befitting a sacred office, applied to older women, showing their share in the clerical inheritance
Inheritance or clerical office, the calling to which women are summoned
Integrity or indifference to corrupting influences, applied to the mind
Dignity or gravity, applied to outward conduct

scripture: The author cites the Epistle to Titus by standard New Testament book name and chapter-verse (e.g., Tit 1:12-13, 1:15-16, 2:3, 2:7). No Old Testament citations appear in the fragments.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is unknown.
The identity of the poet is not named in the source; the attribution to Epimenides is a well-established fact but not stated in the fragment.
The original addressee of the commentary is unknown.

_unresolved_facts.claim: explicitly distancing himself from the poet's false claim about Zeus's tomb
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπιλαμβανόμενος αὐτῶν εἶπεν ὡς κακῶς δεικνύντων τάφον ∆ιὸς τὸν οὐκ ὄντα
_unresolved_facts.fix: The poet claimed to show a tomb of Zeus that did not exist; Severianus says the poet 'lied defending Zeus' (ἐκεῖνος ἐψεύσατο τῷ ∆ιῒ συνηγορῶν), not that the poet denied Zeus's immortality. The poet's claim was false, but the source frames it as the poet defending Zeus by showing a tomb (thereby denying his immortality), not as the poet making a claim about immortality directly.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He interprets Paul's instruction to older women as showing that women are called to a clerical inheritance
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἔδειξεν ὅτι εἰς κλῆρον τὰς γυναῖκας καλεῖ· οὐ γὰρ ἂν ἱεροπρεπεῖς εἶπεν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Severianus says Paul 'showed that he calls women to a lot/portion/inheritance (κλῆρον)' — the term κλῆρος can mean 'clergy' in later Christian usage, but in this context it more naturally means a 'share' or 'portion' in the Christian community. The brief's 'clerical inheritance' over-interprets; the source does not specify 'clerical'.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He quotes the lemma about those who profess to know God but deny him by works
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: καὶ τοῦτό ἐστι τὸ θεὸν ὁμολογοῦσιν εἰδέναι, τοῖς δὲ ἔργοις ἀρνοῦνται
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source only quotes the lemma without any interpretive comment from Severianus; there is no 'argument' here, just the quotation. The outline incorrectly suggests Severianus argues something about this verse in this section.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Severianus notes the poet 'lied defending Zeus'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source says the poet 'lied defending Zeus' (τῷ ∆ιῒ συνηγορῶν), but this is Severianus's characterization of the poet's action, not a claim about what the poet said about Zeus's immortality. The brief's description conflates the poet's false claim (showing a tomb) with Severianus's evaluation of it.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Quoted directly in the lemma from Titus 1:12 as 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, idle gluttons'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐπειδὴ ὁ ποιητὴς ὁ εἰρηκὼς τὸ Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί
_unresolved_facts.fix: The poet's words are embedded in Severianus's paraphrase, not marked as a direct quotation with quotation marks or formula. The brief's 'Quoted directly' overstates the presentation; it's a paraphrased embedding in Severianus's commentary.
